name: Test Pyramid and Where to Test
intent: Choose how many unit, integration and end-to-end tests to write by asking where each kind of bug can be seen, how fast the test runs and how often it fails for no reason.
scenario: A shop app has eight known bugs: three in pricing logic, three where components meet (database columns, an API unit, a payment timeout) and two in user journeys. The team compares a suite of many unit tests, a mix with a middle layer, one heavy on browser tests, and a suite of unit tests only.
problem: The pyramid is usually drawn as many cheap unit tests, fewer integration tests and a handful of end-to-end tests, and it is read as a rule about shape. The shape is a consequence, not the point. Each kind of test sees a different class of bug, and costs a different amount to run and to keep stable. A suite of 200 unit tests can be fast, green and still miss every bug that lives between two components. A suite of browser tests can catch almost everything and still be useless, because it is slow and fails by itself so often that a red build stops meaning anything. The question is not which layer is best, it is where each bug can be seen at the lowest cost.

howItWorks.title: List the bugs you fear, by where they live
howItWorks.text: Some bugs live inside one function: a rounding rule, a boundary. Some live where two parts meet: a column mapped to the wrong field, a unit mismatch between services, a timeout. Some only exist in a user journey: a button wired to the wrong handler, a session lost on redirect. Naming where a bug lives tells you which kind of test could ever see it.

howItWorks.title: Put each check at the cheapest layer that can see it
howItWorks.text: A unit test runs one piece of logic in memory, so it is fast and points at the line. An integration test runs real components together, such as the service against a real database, so it can see mapping and configuration bugs but is slower. An end-to-end test drives the whole system the way a user does, so it sees journeys but is the slowest and the most fragile. Write a check at the lowest layer that can reveal the bug.

howItWorks.title: Count the cost of each layer
howItWorks.text: Cost has three parts: time to run, effort to keep working when the app changes, and the rate of false failures. A test that fails on its own a few times in a hundred runs, such as one that depends on a browser, a network and a clock, makes a big suite red most of the time. Typical figures differ a lot between projects, so measure your own.

howItWorks.title: Keep a few tests that cross the layers
howItWorks.text: Unit tests with the collaborators replaced cannot show that the pieces fit. A few integration tests over the real seams and a small number of end-to-end tests for the journeys that must never break close that gap. Teams that prefer a trophy shape, with most tests at the integration layer, accept slower tests for more realism. Teams that prefer a pyramid accept more replaced collaborators for speed.

howItWorks.title: Review the mix when bugs escape
howItWorks.text: Each production bug is a question: which layer could have caught it, and why did it not? Add the test at that layer. If bugs keep escaping from one layer, or a layer produces more false alarms than real finds, change the mix rather than adding more of the same.

pros: Cheap, fast unit tests give quick feedback and point at the failing line
A few integration and end-to-end tests cover bugs that only appear when the parts are joined
Knowing the cost of each layer lets a team set a budget for slow tests
Thinking in layers explains why a green suite can still ship a bug
cons: The ratios are folklore: the right mix depends on the app, and teams disagree between the pyramid and the trophy
Unit tests with replaced collaborators can all pass while the real parts do not fit
Layers cost more to maintain as they get higher, and reviewers rarely see that cost
A bug can fall between layers, so each owner assumes someone else tests it
whenToUse: Planning the test strategy of a new service or a rewrite
A green suite keeps letting the same class of bug reach production
The suite has become slow or flaky and the team must decide what to cut
whenNotToUse: As a fixed ratio to copy: the numbers in this lesson come from a toy model, not from your code
To argue that one layer is useless: each can see bugs the others cannot
For code that is mostly glue and configuration, where a few integration tests tell you more than many unit tests
pitfalls: 200 unit tests, all green, and the bugs between components still ship, because unit tests never exercise the seams
The ice-cream cone: dozens of browser tests, a suite that takes hours and fails on its own so often that people re-run until it is green
Testing a login redirect with a mocked session and calling the journey covered
Treating a red build as noise after many false alarms, then missing the one that was real
Adding an end-to-end test for every bug, because it feels realistic, when a unit test would find it in a millisecond
Counting tests instead of asking which bugs can reach users through the gaps

roles.label: Developer
roles.description: Writes the code and the fast tests next to it.

roles.label: Unit tests
roles.description: Run one piece of logic in memory, fast and precise.

roles.label: Integration tests
roles.description: Run real components together, so they can see how the parts meet.

roles.label: End-to-end tests
roles.description: Drive the whole system like a user, slow and the most fragile.

roles.label: Production
roles.description: Where a bug that no test reached ends up.

quiz.question: A suite of 200 unit tests is green, yet the order is saved with swapped database columns. What explains this?
options: Unit tests are unreliable and should be replaced by browser tests.
The 200 tests were too few, and 2,000 would have found it.
The bug lives where code meets the database, which a unit test with a replaced repository never runs.
The tests ran in the wrong order, hiding the failure.
quiz.explanation: A unit test runs one piece of logic in memory, usually with the database replaced. A bug in the mapping between code and database is outside what it exercises, and more tests of the same kind do not change that.

quiz.question: A team has 60 end-to-end tests. They catch most bugs, but 47 of every 50 runs go red with no bug present. What is the main cost?
options: The tests are too accurate, so they report problems nobody can fix.
A red build no longer carries a signal, so real failures are re-run and ignored.
End-to-end tests cannot find bugs in pricing logic at all.
The suite finishes too quickly to be trusted.
quiz.explanation: False failures train people to re-run and merge. The slow, fragile layer is also the one that makes the most noise, which is why the pyramid keeps it small. These tests can see logic bugs, but at a high price.

quiz.question: Which statement about the pyramid and the trophy shapes is closest to the truth?
options: Both are proven ratios, and one of them wins on every project.
The pyramid is outdated, because unit tests never find bugs.
They are two ways to trade speed against realism, and the right mix depends on where your bugs live.
The trophy is only for front-end code, and the pyramid only for back-end code.
quiz.explanation: Practitioners disagree. The pyramid favours speed and precise failures, and accepts more replaced collaborators. The trophy favours realism at the integration layer and accepts slower tests. Neither is a measured rule.
